name: Does an Electric Current Have a Magnetic Effect?

scenes.animation: A school science exhibition. Senior student Sumana closes a switch; an iron nail wrapped in wire and joined to a battery picks up iron paper clips. She opens the switch and the clips drop. Mohini, Aakarsh and Zippy gasp.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Where's the magnet? That nail is just wrapped in wire!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. There's no magnet, only an electric circuit. Let's find out how electricity does a magnet's job.

scenes.animation: Activity 4.1 built step by step: a switch made from two drawing pins, a safety pin and cardboard; a cell in its holder; two nails on cardboard with a wire stretched between them just above the surface; the wire joined to the cell holder and switch; a compass placed beneath the wire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 4.1. Make a switch with two drawing pins, a safety pin and cardboard, and put a cell in a cell holder.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Fix two nails on a cardboard and stretch a long wire between them, slightly above the surface.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Connect the wire to the cell holder and the switch, and place a magnetic compass under the wire.

scenes.animation: Close-up of the compass under the wire. Switch ON: the needle swings sideways. Switch OFF: it swings back. The ON-OFF toggle repeats three times, the needle following each time. Faint circular field lines glow around the wire only when ON.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Switch on, the needle jumps. Switch off, it goes back. It's dancing!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The compass needle is a tiny magnet. Its deflection shows that a current-carrying wire has a magnetic effect.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The region around a magnet or a current-carrying wire where its magnetic effect can be felt is said to have a magnetic field.

scenes.animation: A definition card slides in: 'Magnetic effect of electric current: current in a conductor produces a magnetic field around it'. The field lines vanish as the current stops. Icons of an electric bell, fan, motor and loudspeaker pop up around it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When electric current flows through a conductor like a wire, it produces a magnetic field around it. This is the magnetic effect of electric current.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The magnetic field disappears when the current stops.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This effect is used in electromagnets, electric bells, motors, fans and loudspeakers.

scenes.animation: Sepia 1820 lecture hall in Denmark: Professor Hans Christian Oersted demonstrates a circuit; a compass on his desk twitches each time he closes it. He stares, then scribbles notes. 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Needle deflects only while current flows'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You just repeated a famous discovery. In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted, a professor in Denmark, noticed a nearby compass needle deflect whenever he closed or opened a circuit.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He investigated until he was sure that electric current produces a magnetic field, and then published it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: the needle deflects only while current flows. When the current stops, the needle returns to its original direction.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a compass icon. Points: '1. Current-carrying wire deflects a compass', '2. Current produces a magnetic field: magnetic effect of current', '3. Oersted, 1820: electricity and magnetism are linked'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: a compass needle near a current-carrying wire gets deflected.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: current in a conductor produces a magnetic field around it, which disappears when the current stops.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: Oersted discovered this link between electricity and magnetism in 1820.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Electricity and magnets are secret best friends!

scenes.animation: Zippy drops a box of iron paper clips on the floor. He waves an ordinary iron nail over them; nothing happens. He glares at the nail.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Come on, nail, pick them up! Why won't you work?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because it's not a magnet yet. Let's use electric current to turn it into one.

scenes.animation: Activity 4.2 step by step: 50 cm of flexible insulated wire wound tightly around an iron nail as a coil and taped; the ends touch a cell; the nail lifts clips. A timer icon flashes 'Only a few seconds!' The wire is disconnected and the clips fall.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 4.2. Wrap about 50 centimetres of flexible insulated wire tightly around an iron nail, and tape it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Connect the ends to a cell, but only for a few seconds, or the cell may weaken quickly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Bring the nail near iron paper clips. They cling to it. Disconnect the wire, and they fall.

scenes.animation: Activity 4.3 step by step: chart paper rolled into a pencil-wide cylinder and taped; about 50 turns of 100 cm insulated wire wound on it; two compasses placed at its ends; the coil connected to a cell and both needles deflect.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now Activity 4.3. Roll chart paper into a cylinder about as wide as a pencil.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Wind around 50 turns of insulated wire on it, and place a compass near each end.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Connect the coil to a cell. Both compass needles deflect. The coil behaves like a magnet.

scenes.animation: An iron nail slides into the paper cylinder. The compass needles swing much further, and clips jump to the nail ends. Disconnect: needles return, clips drop. A label builds: 'Electromagnet = current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Whoa, with the nail inside, the needles swing way more!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Right. With an iron nail in the core, the coil becomes a stronger magnet and attracts iron clips. Stop the current, and it loses its magnetic effect.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet is called an electromagnet. Most practical electromagnets have an iron core to make them stronger.

scenes.animation: A side-by-side comparison card: bar magnet 'always magnetic' vs electromagnet 'magnetic only when current flows; switch ON/OFF'. 'Exam Tip' sticker on the words 'iron core'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's the big advantage. An electromagnet works only while current flows, so you can switch its magnetism on and off.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: a coil becomes an electromagnet only when current flows through it. Adding an iron core makes it stronger.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a coil-and-nail icon. Points: '1. Coil + current = electromagnet', '2. Iron core makes it stronger', '3. Magnetism stops when current stops'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: a current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet is an electromagnet.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: an iron core inside the coil makes the electromagnet much stronger.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: when the current stops, the electromagnet loses its magnetism.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My nail finally has superpowers. Part-time ones.

name: Poles, Strength and Uses of Electromagnets

scenes.animation: A scrap yard. A giant crane magnet hovers over a pile of old iron. Zippy sits in the crane cabin with his finger on a big ON/OFF button, grinning.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If I press this button, can I really lift a whole car?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Only if you understand your electromagnet. Let's check its poles and strength first.

scenes.animation: Activity 4.4: the coil ends are labelled A and B. A compass near end A: its north pole swings towards A, so A gets a red 'S' label. The compass moves to end B and its south pole points there; B gets 'N'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 4.4. Label the ends of your electromagnet A and B, and place a compass near end A.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Unlike poles attract. So if the north pole of the compass is attracted to end A, then end A is a south pole.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Repeat at end B, and you find the opposite pole. Just like a bar magnet, an electromagnet has a north and a south pole.

scenes.animation: A control panel with three dials: 'Cells: 1, 2, 4', 'Turns of coil', 'Direction of current'. Turning up cells and turns makes more clips jump on and the compass swing further. Flipping the direction swaps the N and S labels.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A single cell gives a small current, so the field is weak and only a few clips are attracted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A battery with more cells gives a larger current and a stronger field. More turns in the coil also make it stronger.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And if you reverse the direction of the current, the poles get reversed.

scenes.animation: Back at the scrap yard: current ON, the crane electromagnet lifts a heap of iron and steel; current OFF, the heap drops into a sorting bin. Then a quick cut to Earth with a glowing liquid-iron core and field lines, a flock of migratory birds following them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Lifting electromagnets are strong electromagnets hung from cranes. Current on, they lift iron and steel objects. Current off, the field disappears and the objects are released.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Factories and scrap yards use them to move, lift and sort heavy metal items.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Even Earth behaves like a magnet. Moving liquid iron in its core creates electric currents, which generate a magnetic field that migratory birds use to navigate.

scenes.animation: An 'Exam Tip' card lists 'Strength ↑: more current, more turns' and 'Poles reverse: reverse current'. A crossed-out statement: 'Single cell attracts more clips than 2 cells'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So one cell beats two cells, because it's gentler?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No! Exam tip: more current or more turns makes a stronger electromagnet. Two cells attract more clips than one. Reversing the current reverses the poles.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a crane icon. Points: '1. Electromagnet has N and S poles', '2. Strength depends on current and number of turns', '3. Lifting electromagnets: switch ON to lift, OFF to release'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: an electromagnet has a north and a south pole, which reverse when the current reverses.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: its strength increases with more current or more turns of the coil.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: lifting electromagnets on cranes lift iron when switched on and drop it when switched off.

scenes.animation: A chilly winter morning. Mummy plugs in an electric kettle for chai; Zippy watches steam rise and peers at the heating coil glowing red in an old room heater.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: There's no fire in the kettle. So how is the chai water boiling?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Electric current itself can make heat. Let's test it with a special wire.

scenes.animation: Activity 4.5 step by step, with a 'Teacher supervision' badge: a 10 cm by 10 cm cardboard, two nails about 5 cm apart, a 10 cm nichrome wire about 0.3 mm thick tied between them, a cell, holder and switch in OFF position. A finger touches the cold wire first.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 4.5 must be done under a teacher's supervision. Tie a nichrome wire, about 10 centimetres long, between two nails on a cardboard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Connect it to a cell through a switch, kept OFF. Touch the wire. It feels normal.

scenes.animation: The switch goes ON for 30 seconds, a timer counting. Switch OFF, a finger taps the wire for just a moment and pulls back; heat wavy lines rise. A bold 'Safety First: touch only momentarily, don't hold the wire' banner flashes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now switch it ON for about 30 seconds, then OFF. Touch the wire only for a moment. Do not hold it, and never touch it for long.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Ouch, it's warm!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Current faces opposition, called resistance, as it flows through a conductor. Resistance converts some electrical energy into heat energy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This is the heating effect of electric current. Nichrome offers higher resistance than a copper wire of the same size and length.

scenes.animation: Two setups side by side: one cell vs a battery of two cells; the two-cell wire glows warmer. A list builds: 'Heat depends on: current, material, thickness, length, time'. Then appliances pop up: room heater, electric stove, kettle, iron, immersion rod, hair dryer, each with a glowing 'heating element'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: With two cells, the wire heats up more, because heat depends on the amount of current.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Heat also depends on the wire's material, thickness, length, and how long the current flows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Room heaters, electric stoves, kettles, irons, immersion rods and hair dryers all have a heating element, a rod or coil of wire, that works on this effect.

scenes.animation: A switchboard with a melting plastic plug and a small flame; then a correctly rated plug and socket with a green tick. A steel furnace melts scrap into glowing new steel. 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Nichrome = more heat for a given current'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Heating can also cause problems. Overheating can melt plastic parts of plugs and sockets, or even cause fires. So use wires, plugs and sockets rated for the current.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In industry, electric furnaces melt and recycle scrap steel.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: nichrome is used in heaters because it generates more heat for a given current.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a kettle icon. Points: '1. Resistance turns electrical energy into heat', '2. Heat depends on current, material, thickness, length, time', '3. Heating element in heaters, kettles, irons'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: a conductor gets heated when current passes through it. This is the heating effect of electric current.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: heat depends on current, the wire's material, thickness and length, and time.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: heaters, kettles and irons use a heating element, but overheating can cause fires.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Chai powered by resistance. Respect!

name: Voltaic Cell and the Lemon Battery

scenes.animation: Zippy juggles five lemons in the school canteen. Neo stops him and hands him copper wires, iron nails and a tiny LED.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Nimbu pani for everyone!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Wait. Those lemons can light a lamp. But first, what's inside a cell that makes electricity?

scenes.animation: A glass container fills with liquid labelled 'Electrolyte: weak acid or salt solution'. Two rods of different metals dip in, labelled 'Electrode 1' and 'Electrode 2'. A wire and lamp connect them; current arrows flow from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal. Later the chemicals fade and a 'Dead' stamp appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A Voltaic cell, also called a Galvanic cell, has two rods of different metals partly dipped in a liquid called an electrolyte.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The rods are electrodes. The electrolyte is usually a weak acid or salt solution. A chemical reaction between them produces electricity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal. When the chemicals are used up, the cell is dead.

scenes.animation: Sepia late-1700s Italy: Galvani touches a frog leg with copper and iron and it twitches; he points at the frog. Volta shakes his head, swaps the frog for saltwater-soaked paper, and still gets a spark. A caption: 'Metals + liquid = first battery'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The names come from two Italian scientists. In the late 1700s, Galvani saw a dead frog's leg kick when touched with copper and iron. He thought the electricity came from the frog.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Volta replaced the frog's leg with saltwater-soaked paper and still got current. So the metals and the liquid made it. This led to the first battery.

scenes.animation: Activity 4.6 step by step: a copper wire and an iron nail pushed into one lemon, a little apart; repeated for five lemons; copper of one joined to the nail of the next in a chain; an LED connected between the first copper wire and the last nail. The LED stays dark, gets flipped, then glows. Labels: 'Longer leg: +', 'Shorter leg: −'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 4.6. Push a copper wire and an iron nail into a lemon, a small distance apart. Do this for five or six lemons.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Join the copper wire of each lemon to the nail of the next. Connect an LED between the first copper wire and the last nail.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: It's not glowing. The lemons are broken!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Just reverse the LED. It glows only when its longer, positive leg joins the positive terminal. Here, copper and iron are electrodes, and lemon juice is the electrolyte.

scenes.animation: An 'Exam Tip' card: 'Electrolyte: lemon juice or salt solution helps conduct electricity'. Metal pairs float by: zinc/copper, iron/copper, magnesium/copper.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You can use a salt solution instead of lemon juice. Common metal pairs include zinc and copper, iron and copper, and magnesium and copper.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: the liquid in a Voltaic cell is called an electrolyte, and the cell works because of chemical reactions.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a lemon icon. Points: '1. Voltaic cell: two different metal electrodes + electrolyte', '2. Chemical reaction produces electricity', '3. Lemon cell: copper, iron nail, lemon juice; LED + to +'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: a Voltaic cell has two electrodes of different metals in an electrolyte.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a chemical reaction produces the electricity, and the cell dies when the chemicals are used up.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: a lemon cell uses copper and iron electrodes, with lemon juice as the electrolyte.

scenes.animation: Zippy tries to carry a sloshing glass jar Voltaic cell to power a TV remote; liquid spills everywhere. Neo holds up a small AA dry cell.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My remote needs power, but this jar keeps spilling!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's why Voltaic cells aren't convenient for everyday use. Meet the dry cell.

scenes.animation: A dry cell slices open like a cross-section: outer 'Zinc container: negative terminal', central 'Carbon rod with metal cap: positive terminal', and a thick 'Moist paste electrolyte' around the rod. Labels appear one by one.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dry cells are among the most widely used cells today. They're called dry because the electrolyte is a thick moist paste, not a liquid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A zinc container acts as the negative terminal. A carbon rod at the centre, with a metal cap, is the positive terminal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The paste-like electrolyte surrounds the carbon rod. A dry cell is single use. Once used up, it must be disposed of.

scenes.animation: A parade of rechargeable batteries: watch, phone, laptop, camera, inverter, electric scooter. A phone plugs into a charger; its battery icon fills. A calendar flips two years and the phone needs charging more often.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused many times. This prevents wastage and saves money.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They run watches, phones, laptops, cameras, inverters and even electric vehicles.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So why does my dad's two-year-old phone need charging all the time?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because rechargeable batteries don't last forever. After being charged and used many times, they slowly wear out.

scenes.animation: A globe with mining symbols for 'Lithium' and 'Cobalt' in a few regions. A futuristic 'Solid-state battery' glows with a solid block replacing liquid. Then a used battery hovers over a regular dustbin with a red cross, and moves into an 'E-waste recycling' bin with a green tick.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The lithium-ion battery is the most common rechargeable battery. It uses metals like lithium and cobalt, mined in limited parts of the world.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Scientists are working on solid-state batteries, with solid electrolytes, which would be safer, charge faster and last longer.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A dead battery may still contain acids and metals like lead, cadmium, nickel or lithium. Never throw it in regular garbage. Use an e-waste recycling facility.

scenes.animation: An 'Exam Tip' card with a true/false toggle: 'Dry cells are less portable than Voltaic cells' flips to FALSE with a buzzer. Then 'Dry cell: zinc (−), carbon rod (+)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: dry cells are more portable than Voltaic cells, not less. And remember, zinc is negative and the carbon rod is positive.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a battery icon. Points: '1. Dry cell: zinc (−), carbon rod (+), paste electrolyte', '2. Dry cells are single use; rechargeables are reused', '3. Recycle old batteries as e-waste'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: a dry cell has a zinc container as the negative terminal, a carbon rod as the positive terminal, and a paste electrolyte.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: dry cells are single use, while rechargeable batteries can be reused many times but slowly wear out.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: used batteries must go to e-waste recycling, not regular garbage.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Old batteries deserve a proper farewell!
